screens.title: Route Redistribution and Filtering
screens.narratorSegment: In complex enterprise networks you rarely run a single routing protocol everywhere. Different areas may use EIGRP, OSPF, or BGP for historical or operational reasons. Route redistribution connects these domains by taking routes learned in one protocol and injecting them into another. That capability is essential for end-to-end reachability, but it also creates the most common operational hazards: loops, black holes, and surprising path selection. In this lesson you will learn the protective controls that make redistribution safe. We'll define administrative distance, explain seed metrics used by EIGRP and OSPF, and show how to use filtering tools — distribute lists, prefix lists, and route maps — plus tagging to prevent routes from being re-injected into their origin. As a concrete example, you will see a two-router lab where R1 runs OSPF and R2 runs EIGRP, each advertising a loopback. You will configure two-way redistribution with tags so routes only cross the boundary once. By the end you will know which commands to verify behavior and the common mistakes to test for. Think: how can one simple tag prevent an entire redistribution loop?

screens.title: Learning Objectives — Part 1
screens.narratorSegment: In this first objectives slide I will set the skills you'll practice. First, you will understand why redistribution is necessary in multi-protocol networks and the operational challenges it introduces. That means you'll be able to explain the core risks: loops, black holes, and unexpected path selection. Second, you'll configure one-way and two-way redistribution between EIGRP, OSPF, and BGP in a lab environment. This includes applying seed metrics for EIGRP and selecting OSPF metric-types so redistributed routes carry reasonable cost. Both objectives matter because misconfigured redistribution immediately affects reachability. For example, without an appropriate seed metric, an EIGRP router may install a redistributed OSPF route with an unusable metric, causing traffic to drop. In practice you'll test commands like show ip route and show ip protocols to verify outcomes. Keep in mind a common misconception: redistribution alone does not solve trust — administrative distance and filtering determine which route is actually used. Later you'll practice those controls to avoid surprises.

screens.title: What is Route Redistribution?
screens.narratorSegment: Route redistribution is the mechanical process of taking routes learned in one routing protocol and injecting them into another. It is necessary when parts of a network run different protocols — for example, one department uses EIGRP while the rest of the campus uses OSPF, or an edge uses BGP for internet connectivity. Redistribution restores reachability between these islands by translating and advertising prefixes across protocol boundaries. That translation is not free: protocols use different metrics and trust values, so an injected route needs a seed metric and will be subject to administrative distance when the router chooses which source to install. A common example is importing an OSPF-learned loopback into EIGRP so an EIGRP-only area can reach it. The major risk is routing loops and suboptimal routing when a route is learned back into its original domain. To mitigate this you will use tags to mark the origin and filters to prevent re-injection. Remember, redistribution gives connectivity but demands deliberate controls. A good closing question: after you redistribute a route, how will you ensure it is preferred in the right domain and not accidentally reintroduced as an inferior or loop-causing path?

keyIdea.title: Definition
keyIdea.text: Redistribution moves routing information between protocols; it restores reachability but can create loops without filters and tags.

content.html:
Core Concept Definition
Route Redistribution — clear definition
Taking routes learned by one routing protocol and advertising them into another so hosts in different protocol domains can reach each other.
When it's used
Migrations, acquisitions, or mixed protocol deployments where full conversion is not feasible.
Primary risk
Routing loops and suboptimal routes if tags, AD, or filtering are not applied.
Practical example
Import an OSPF loopback into EIGRP so EIGRP-only routers learn the network.
Analogy & takeaway
Think of redistribution as translating between two languages. If you translate and then translate back without marking the translation, you can create confusion and duplicates. Tags act like a watermark that identifies translated routes.
Key Takeaway

Redistribution is powerful but must be paired with filtering, metrics, and tagging to avoid loops and broken reachability.

Check your understanding
What marker would you apply to an imported route so it can be identified later? (Hint: tags)

screens.title: Administrative Distance (AD)
screens.narratorSegment: Administrative distance is the router's trust ranking for route sources. Each routing protocol has a default AD value — lower means more trusted. For instance, EIGRP internal typically uses 90, OSPF internal 110, and external BGP 20. When the router learns the same prefix from multiple protocols, it installs the route with the lowest AD into the IP routing table. In the context of redistribution, AD determines which copy of a redistributed prefix wins. A problematic scenario occurs when routes are redistributed across domains and the redistributed copy has a lower AD than the native copy, causing the router to prefer the redistributed path and potentially create loops. To control this, operators can change AD with the distance command under routing processes or with set distance in a route map. A misconception is that metrics alone decide selection; metrics affect protocol-internal calculations, but AD controls which protocol's route is installed first. Example: if the same prefix appears via OSPF and EIGRP, the EIGRP-learned route may be chosen because its AD is lower. Ask yourself: after redistributing, which AD will the receiving router prefer, and do you need to change it?

keyIdea.title: AD impact
keyIdea.text: Administrative distance determines which protocol's route appears in the routing table when duplicates exist; adjust it if redistribution changes preferred paths.

content.html:
Definition Administrative Distance
What AD is and how routers use it
  • AD is a trust value assigned to a route source; lower values win.
  • Common defaults: EIGRP internal 90, OSPF internal 110, BGP external 20.
  • AD controls which route is installed when multiple sources advertise the same prefix.
Practical implications
After redistribution, check which AD each route will have on receivers. If the redistributed route becomes the preferred path unexpectedly, consider changing AD or filtering the route.
Common misconception
Assuming metrics alone determine selection. Metrics influence internal protocol path choice, but AD decides which protocol's route is placed in the routing table.
Key Takeaway

Always check administrative distances after redistribution and adjust or filter to enforce the intended path.

screens.title: Seed Metrics and OSPF Metric-Type
screens.narratorSegment: When a route is redistributed into a new protocol, it often lacks a native metric for that protocol. A seed metric gives the route a usable cost on the target protocol. For EIGRP, you must set bandwidth, delay, reliability, load, and MTU values with the redistribute command so the external route is attractive and usable. If you forget a default metric, redistributed routes can be ignored or appear suboptimal. For OSPF, there is an additional concept: metric-type. OSPF external Type 1 adds the internal OSPF path cost to the external metric, while Type 2 uses only the external metric for ranking. Type 2 is commonly preferred when you want the external metric to dominate regardless of internal path cost. A concrete example: redistributing EIGRP routes into OSPF with Type 1 may make the internal OSPF distance influence selection; choose Type 2 when you need consistent external preference. A common mistake is neglecting the seed metric or forgetting the subnets keyword when redistributing classless networks into OSPF. Ask: does the redistributed metric make the route usable for your traffic patterns? Seed Metrics and OSPF Metric-Type means assign appropriate seed metrics for redistributed routes; choose ospf metric-type to control how internal costs affect external routes.. In practical terms, why redistributed routes need metrics and how ospf handles external metrics. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

content.html:
Seed Metric Metric and OSPF types
EIGRP seed metric
When redistributing into EIGRP set a metric like: bandwidth, delay, reliability, load, MTU so the route is usable within EIGRP's composite metric.
Why it matters
Without a seed metric, redistributed routes may be ignored or receive an unusable default metric.
OSPF metric-type
  • Type 1: external metric plus internal OSPF cost (adds internal cost).
  • Type 2: uses only the external metric (internal cost ignored for external routes).
Common mistake
Omitting the subnets keyword when redistributing into OSPF prevents classless prefixes from being advertised.
Key Takeaway

Always set appropriate seed metrics and pick OSPF metric-type to match your reachability goals; test redistributed route usability immediately.

screens.title: Redistribute Commands — Practical Syntax
screens.narratorSegment: Let's look at concrete redistribute commands you will use in the lab. When redistributing into EIGRP you commonly include a metric argument to set bandwidth, delay, reliability, load, and MTU. That seed metric ensures the route is usable inside EIGRP. For OSPF, when redistributing into OSPF, include the subnets keyword to advertise classless networks and choose metric-type for external routes. Here is a focused example line taken from the scenario: redistribute ospf 100 metric 10000 100 255 1 1500 route-map SET_OSPF_TAG. This command runs under router eigrp 200 and tells EIGRP to import OSPF routes using the given composite metric and apply a route map to set tags. A common practical step: attach a route map that sets a tag immediately so any subsequent redistribution can deny matching tagged routes. As you type these commands in a lab, remember to verify with show ip route and show ip protocols to confirm the routes appear and carry the expected tags. A misconception to avoid is trusting redistribution without verification — always test the route's metric and AD after configuration. keyIdea.text: Use redistribute with appropriate metric arguments and route maps to set tags; verify the resulting route attributes with show commands.

content.html:
Configuration Code walkthrough 
! Example: R2 redistributing OSPF into EIGRP (snippet)
router eigrp 200
 network 2.2.2.0 0.0.0.255
 network 10.0.0.0 0.0.0.255
 redistribute ospf 100 metric 10000 100 255 1 1500 route-map SET_OSPF_TAG

route-map SET_OSPF_TAG permit 10
 set tag 100
Explanation
  • redistribute ospf 100 — imports OSPF routes from process 100.
  • metric 10000 100 255 1 1500 — EIGRP seed metric values to make the route usable.
  • route-map SET_OSPF_TAG — applies a tag so routes are identifiable later.
Pro tip
Set the tag at ingestion time so subsequent redistributions can match and deny tagged routes.

screens.title: Filtering Tools Compared
screens.narratorSegment: Filtering redistributed routes is essential to control what crosses protocol boundaries. There are three primary tools, each with strengths. Distribute lists are the simplest: they use access-lists to permit or deny prefixes on a routing process or an interface. They are quick and easy but lack length/mask granularity. Prefix lists are designed for prefix-based filtering; they can match by network and mask length ranges and are more efficient and expressive than access lists for route control. Route maps are the most powerful: they let you combine matches against prefix lists, access lists, AS path, or tags and then set attributes such as metric, tag, or administrative distance. Route maps are commonly applied to redistribute commands so you can both filter and transform attributes in one place. A practical pattern is to use prefix lists to match the prefixes you want and a route map to set tags and deny tagged routes on the reverse redistribution. A common misconception is that one filtering method is always sufficient; in practice you often combine prefix lists for matching with route maps for action.

keyIdea.title: Filter selection
keyIdea.text: Use prefix lists for precise matching and route maps for matched actions like tagging or metric manipulation; distribute lists are simplest but less granular.

content.html:
Comparison Filtering tools
Distribute List
Quick permit/deny using standard or extended access-lists. Applied inbound/outbound to processes or interfaces.
Use when: simple inclusion/exclusion is sufficient.
Prefix List
Match network prefixes with mask length control using ge/le operators. Efficient and explicit.
Use when: you need mask-length precision.
Route Map
Combine matches and set attributes: metrics, tags, and administrative distance. Can both filter and transform.
Use when: you need conditional logic or attribute manipulation.
Key Takeaway

Combine tools: use prefix lists to precisely match prefixes, then a route map to tag or set metrics so you can safely control redistribution direction and behavior.

screens.title: Tagging Strategy to Prevent Loops
screens.narratorSegment: A reliable pattern for two-way redistribution is tag-and-deny. The idea is simple and powerful: when importing routes from Protocol A into Protocol B, set a unique tag on those routes. When importing from Protocol B back into Protocol A, use a route map to deny any routes that carry Protocol A's tag. The process is: first, identify which prefixes to redistribute and craft a prefix list. Second, create a route map that on permit sets a distinguishing tag and optionally sets a seed metric. Third, apply that route map on the redistribute command for the target protocol. Fourth, create the reciprocal route map on the other router or protocol to explicitly deny routes matching the tag. Finally, verify with show ip route and check tags. This prevents a route that originated in A from being re-injected into A after it traverses B. A common misconception is believing that filtering alone without tagging is sufficient; tags provide a reliable identity that survives across routing protocol translations. Try to answer: in your topology, what tag values will you set for each protocol so they remain unique?

keyIdea.title: Tag-and-deny
keyIdea.text: Assign tags to imported routes and deny those tags on reverse redistribution to stop routes crossing the boundary twice.

content.html:
Process Flow Tagging pattern
  1. Create prefix list of prefixes to redistribute.
  2. Define route map: match prefix list, set tag and seed metric.
  3. Apply route map on redistribute command when importing into the other protocol.
  4. On the reverse redistribution, use route map to deny routes with the originating tag.
  5. Verify with show ip route and check tags to ensure no re-injection occurs.
Example snippet (conceptual)
When redistributing OSPF into EIGRP, set tag 100. When redistributing EIGRP into OSPF, deny tag 100 to stop reinjection.
Common mistake
Forgetting to tag at the point of redistribution, which makes later filtering brittle or impossible.

screens.title: Two-Router Lab — R1 (OSPF) and R2 (EIGRP)
screens.narratorSegment: Now we walk through the two-router lab configuration that ties earlier concepts together. R1 runs OSPF 100 and advertises Loopback0 1.1.1.0/24. R2 runs EIGRP 200 and advertises Loopback0 2.2.2.0/24. They share a common segment 10.0.0.0/24. The goal is two-way redistribution with tags: when R2 redistributes OSPF into EIGRP it sets tag 100; when R1 redistributes EIGRP into OSPF it sets tag 200. Each router then includes route-map entries that deny routes carrying the opposite tag so a route will not be bounced back. After configuration, verify that R1 learns 2.2.2.0/24 as an OSPF external route and that R2 learns 1.1.1.0/24 as an EIGRP external route, and that neither route is reintroduced into its origin. Use show ip route ospf and show ip route eigrp to check. A common error is omitting the set tag lines or forgetting subnets for OSPF redistribution. When you test, ensure the tags appear and the denied routes are absent from the reverse protocol's external table. keyIdea.title: Lab config
keyIdea.text: Implement two-way redistribution with set tags and deny tagged routes on the opposite redistribution; verify expected external routes and absent reinjections.

content.html:
Hands-on Lab Two-router example 
! Router R1 (OSPF 100)
hostname R1
interface Loopback0
 ip address 1.1.1.1 255.255.255.0
interface GigabitEthernet0/0
 ip address 10.0.0.1 255.255.255.0
route-map SET_EIGRP_TAG permit 10
 set tag 200
route-map EIGRP_TO_OSPF deny 20
router ospf 100
 router-id 1.1.1.1
 network 1.1.1.0 0.0.0.255 area 0
 network 10.0.0.0 0.0.0.255 area 0
 redistribute eigrp 200 subnets route-map SET_EIGRP_TAG

! Router R2 (EIGRP 200)
hostname R2
interface Loopback0
 ip address 2.2.2.2 255.255.255.0
interface GigabitEthernet0/0
 ip address 10.0.0.2 255.255.255.0
route-map SET_OSPF_TAG permit 10
 set tag 100
route-map OSPF_TO_EIGRP deny 20
router eigrp 200
 network 2.2.2.0 0.0.0.255
 network 10.0.0.0 0.0.0.255
 redistribute ospf 100 metric 10000 100 255 1 1500 route-map SET_OSPF_TAG
 no auto-summary
Verification steps
  • On R1: show ip route ospf — confirm 2.2.2.0/24 appears as OSPF external and check tag.
  • On R2: show ip route eigrp — confirm 1.1.1.0/24 appears as EIGRP external and check tag.
  • Ensure 1.1.1.0/24 is not an EIGRP external on R1 and 2.2.2.0/24 not an OSPF external on R2.
Key Takeaway

Tags plus route maps provide a reliable, local mechanism to prevent redistribution loops during two-way exchanges.

screens.title: Common Mistakes and How to Test
screens.narratorSegment: When implementing redistribution, several recurring mistakes cause outages. First, forgetting a default or seed metric for EIGRP or OSPF will make redistributed routes unattractive or invisible. Always set the metric on redistribute into EIGRP and include subnets when redistributing into OSPF. Second, overlooking administrative distance means a redistributed route might be preferred incorrectly. Check which protocol's route is installed and adjust AD if necessary. Third, failing to tag and deny allows two-way redistribution loops. The lab pattern of set tag on import and deny the tag on reverse redistribution is the most robust fix. How do you test? Start with show ip route to see which routes appear and their sources. Use show ip protocols to view redistribution statements and route-maps. Show route-map or show run | section route-map to verify configuration. Use debug only in a controlled lab. A practical test sequence: apply redistribution, then immediately run show ip route for the target prefix, inspect the tag and metric, then verify the reverse side lacks reintroduced prefixes. screens.title: Design Patterns for Redistribution
screens.narratorSegment: Design choices around where to perform redistribution affect complexity and risk. Two common patterns are centralized redistribution and peer-by-peer redistribution. Centralized redistribution funnels translations through a single boundary router, which simplifies tag management and policy enforcement but can create a single point of failure and scale challenges. Peer-by-peer redistribution distributes responsibility across multiple routers, which can reduce single-point failures but increases the risk of inconsistent tagging and filter rules and raises the chance of loops. In large enterprises, operators often centralize redistribution at controlled borders and use route maps and prefix lists to limit what is translated. Always document which prefixes cross boundaries and where tags originate. A common misconception is assuming decentralized redistribution is always more resilient; it can be more fragile if filters and tags are not consistently applied. When designing, weigh operational control and verification overhead. Reflection: which pattern better matches your team’s operational discipline and testing capabilities? Design Patterns for Redistribution means centralize to simplify policy and tagging; distribute only if you can maintain consistent filters and verification across peers.. Architecture Design patterns
Centralized Redistribution
A single border router handles all translations. Pros: consistent tags and filters; easier auditing. Cons: single point of policy failure and scaling limits.
Best for
Environments with strict change control and a small set of boundary routers.
Peer-by-Peer Redistribution
Multiple routers perform redistribution locally. Pros: distributed resilience. Cons: higher operational overhead to keep tags and filters consistent.
Best for
Teams with strong automation and consistent policy enforcement across devices.
Key Takeaway

Choose the pattern that matches your operational discipline. If you centralize, make the border router policy-rich; if you distribute, automate filters and tags consistently.

screens.title: Verification Commands and Interpretation
screens.narratorSegment: Verification is the final and crucial step after configuration. Use show ip route to see the installed route and its protocol source. fullNarratorScript:
In complex enterprise networks you rarely run a single routing protocol everywhere. Different areas may use EIGRP, OSPF, or BGP for historical or operational reasons. Route redistribution connects these domains by taking routes learned in one protocol and injecting them into another. That capability is essential for end-to-end reachability, but it also creates the most common operational hazards: loops, black holes, and surprising path selection. In this lesson you will learn the protective controls that make redistribution safe. We'll define administrative distance, explain seed metrics used by EIGRP and OSPF, and show how to use filtering tools — distribute lists, prefix lists, and route maps — plus tagging to prevent routes from being re-injected into their origin. As a concrete example, you will see a two-router lab where R1 runs OSPF and R2 runs EIGRP, each advertising a loopback. You will configure two-way redistribution with tags so routes only cross the boundary once. By the end you will know which commands to verify behavior and the common mistakes to test for. Think: how can one simple tag prevent an entire redistribution loop?

In this first objectives slide I will set the skills you'll practice. First, you will understand why redistribution is necessary in multi-protocol networks and the operational challenges it introduces. That means you'll be able to explain the core risks: loops, black holes, and unexpected path selection. Second, you'll configure one-way and two-way redistribution between EIGRP, OSPF, and BGP in a lab environment. This includes applying seed metrics for EIGRP and selecting OSPF metric-types so redistributed routes carry reasonable cost. Both objectives matter because misconfigured redistribution immediately affects reachability. For example, without an appropriate seed metric, an EIGRP router may install a redistributed OSPF route with an unusable metric, causing traffic to drop. In practice you'll test commands like show ip route and show ip protocols to verify outcomes. Keep in mind a common misconception: redistribution alone does not solve trust — administrative distance and filtering determine which route is actually used. Later you'll practice those controls to avoid surprises.

On this second objectives slide we'll focus on the practical tools and verification steps. You will be able to implement route filtering using distribute lists, prefix lists, and route maps. Route maps are particularly important because they let you match prefixes or tags and set attributes such as metrics and tags on redistributed routes. You'll learn to tag redistributed routes and then deny them when redistributing in the opposite direction — a precise technique that prevents two-way redistribution loops. You'll also learn to interpret administrative distance when multiple protocols advertise the same prefix, so the router chooses the intended path. Lastly, you will practice verification and troubleshooting commands: show ip route, show ip protocols, and cautious use of debugging. A common misconception is relying solely on filtering without checking administrative distance. You will learn to combine AD adjustments, route maps, and tags for a reliable outcome.

Route redistribution is the mechanical process of taking routes learned in one routing protocol and injecting them into another. It is necessary when parts of a network run different protocols — for example, one department uses EIGRP while the rest of the campus uses OSPF, or an edge uses BGP for internet connectivity. Redistribution restores reachability between these islands by translating and advertising prefixes across protocol boundaries. That translation is not free: protocols use different metrics and trust values, so an injected route needs a seed metric and will be subject to administrative distance when the router chooses which source to install. A common example is importing an OSPF-learned loopback into EIGRP so an EIGRP-only area can reach it. The major risk is routing loops and suboptimal routing when a route is learned back into its original domain. To mitigate this you will use tags to mark the origin and filters to prevent re-injection. Remember, redistribution gives connectivity but demands deliberate controls. A good closing question: after you redistribute a route, how will you ensure it is preferred in the right domain and not accidentally reintroduced as an inferior or loop-causing path?

Administrative distance is the router's trust ranking for route sources. Each routing protocol has a default AD value — lower means more trusted. For instance, EIGRP internal typically uses 90, OSPF internal 110, and external BGP 20. When the router learns the same prefix from multiple protocols, it installs the route with the lowest AD into the IP routing table. In the context of redistribution, AD determines which copy of a redistributed prefix wins. A problematic scenario occurs when routes are redistributed across domains and the redistributed copy has a lower AD than the native copy, causing the router to prefer the redistributed path and potentially create loops. To control this, operators can change AD with the distance command under routing processes or with set distance in a route map. A misconception is that metrics alone decide selection; metrics affect protocol-internal calculations, but AD controls which protocol's route is installed first. Example: if the same prefix appears via OSPF and EIGRP, the EIGRP-learned route may be chosen because its AD is lower. Ask yourself: after redistributing, which AD will the receiving router prefer, and do you need to change it?

When a route is redistributed into a new protocol, it often lacks a native metric for that protocol. A seed metric gives the route a usable cost on the target protocol. For EIGRP, you must set bandwidth, delay, reliability, load, and MTU values with the redistribute command so the external route is attractive and usable. If you forget a default metric, redistributed routes can be ignored or appear suboptimal. For OSPF, there is an additional concept: metric-type. OSPF external Type 1 adds the internal OSPF path cost to the external metric, while Type 2 uses only the external metric for ranking. Type 2 is commonly preferred when you want the external metric to dominate regardless of internal path cost. A concrete example: redistributing EIGRP routes into OSPF with Type 1 may make the internal OSPF distance influence selection; choose Type 2 when you need consistent external preference. A common mistake is neglecting the seed metric or forgetting the subnets keyword when redistributing classless networks into OSPF. Ask: does the redistributed metric make the route usable for your traffic patterns? Seed Metrics and OSPF Metric-Type means assign appropriate seed metrics for redistributed routes; choose ospf metric-type to control how internal costs affect external routes.. In practical terms, why redistributed routes need metrics and how ospf handles external metrics. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

Let's look at concrete redistribute commands you will use in the lab. When redistributing into EIGRP you commonly include a metric argument to set bandwidth, delay, reliability, load, and MTU. That seed metric ensures the route is usable inside EIGRP. For OSPF, when redistributing into OSPF, include the subnets keyword to advertise classless networks and choose metric-type for external routes. Here is a focused example line taken from the scenario: redistribute ospf 100 metric 10000 100 255 1 1500 route-map SET_OSPF_TAG. This command runs under router eigrp 200 and tells EIGRP to import OSPF routes using the given composite metric and apply a route map to set tags. A common practical step: attach a route map that sets a tag immediately so any subsequent redistribution can deny matching tagged routes. As you type these commands in a lab, remember to verify with show ip route and show ip protocols to confirm the routes appear and carry the expected tags. A misconception to avoid is trusting redistribution without verification — always test the route's metric and AD after configuration. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

Filtering redistributed routes is essential to control what crosses protocol boundaries. There are three primary tools, each with strengths. Distribute lists are the simplest: they use access-lists to permit or deny prefixes on a routing process or an interface. They are quick and easy but lack length/mask granularity. Prefix lists are designed for prefix-based filtering; they can match by network and mask length ranges and are more efficient and expressive than access lists for route control. Route maps are the most powerful: they let you combine matches against prefix lists, access lists, AS path, or tags and then set attributes such as metric, tag, or administrative distance. Route maps are commonly applied to redistribute commands so you can both filter and transform attributes in one place. A practical pattern is to use prefix lists to match the prefixes you want and a route map to set tags and deny tagged routes on the reverse redistribution. A common misconception is that one filtering method is always sufficient; in practice you often combine prefix lists for matching with route maps for action.

A reliable pattern for two-way redistribution is tag-and-deny. The idea is simple and powerful: when importing routes from Protocol A into Protocol B, set a unique tag on those routes. When importing from Protocol B back into Protocol A, use a route map to deny any routes that carry Protocol A's tag. The process is: first, identify which prefixes to redistribute and craft a prefix list. Second, create a route map that on permit sets a distinguishing tag and optionally sets a seed metric. Third, apply that route map on the redistribute command for the target protocol. Fourth, create the reciprocal route map on the other router or protocol to explicitly deny routes matching the tag. Finally, verify with show ip route and check tags. This prevents a route that originated in A from being re-injected into A after it traverses B. A common misconception is believing that filtering alone without tagging is sufficient; tags provide a reliable identity that survives across routing protocol translations. Try to answer: in your topology, what tag values will you set for each protocol so they remain unique?

Now we walk through the two-router lab configuration that ties earlier concepts together. R1 runs OSPF 100 and advertises Loopback0 1.1.1.0/24. R2 runs EIGRP 200 and advertises Loopback0 2.2.2.0/24. They share a common segment 10.0.0.0/24. The goal is two-way redistribution with tags: when R2 redistributes OSPF into EIGRP it sets tag 100; when R1 redistributes EIGRP into OSPF it sets tag 200. Each router then includes route-map entries that deny routes carrying the opposite tag so a route will not be bounced back. After configuration, verify that R1 learns 2.2.2.0/24 as an OSPF external route and that R2 learns 1.1.1.0/24 as an EIGRP external route, and that neither route is reintroduced into its origin. Use show ip route ospf and show ip route eigrp to check. A common error is omitting the set tag lines or forgetting subnets for OSPF redistribution. When you test, ensure the tags appear and the denied routes are absent from the reverse protocol's external table. Verification is the final and crucial step after configuration. Use show ip route to see the installed route and its protocol source. The route entry will indicate whether it is an external route (for example OSPF E2 or E1) or an external EIGRP route. To inspect a route map's logic, use show run | section route-map or show route-map to view matches and sets. If a route is missing or appears with an unexpected metric or protocol, check whether a seed metric was set or whether administrative distance caused a different protocol's route to be preferred. Let's summarize three essential concepts to remember. First, route redistribution exchanges routes between different protocols but introduces risks such as loops and suboptimal paths. Always treat redistribution as a controlled translation, not a free pass to merge domains. Second, administrative distance decides which protocol's route is installed when duplicates exist. AD can override internal metric preferences, so check and adjust AD when redistribution changes route sources. Third, seed metrics are required when importing routes into protocols that need metrics; setting them correctly ensures redistributed routes are usable. Each concept links to one practical action: apply filters and tags, verify AD, and set seed metrics. Keep these three ideas in mind as you design or implement redistribution in labs and production. Finish with three operational tools and a quick checklist. First, prefix lists give precise control over which prefixes are permitted or denied during redistribution, especially when mask lengths matter. Second, route maps combine matching and setting actions: match prefixes or tags and set metrics, tags, or administrative distance. Third, route tagging is the practical technique that prevents routes from being redistributed back into their originating protocol. Your final checklist before deploying redistribution should include: set a seed metric, apply a tag on imported routes, deny tagged routes on reverse redistribution, and verify with show ip route and show ip protocols.
